pos: n. phrase (the shepherd's two implements in Psalm 23:4 — the club that defends and the crook that guides)
etymology: Hebrew shebet, a rod or club, and mishenet, a staff to lean on — from shaan, to support. Two different tools, and the psalm names both because they do different work.
biblical_def: The rod and staff are the shepherd's gear: “Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil: for thou art with me; thy rod and thy staff they comfort me” (Psa 23:4). The rod is a weapon and a mark of rule: “he shall rule them with a rod of iron” (Rev 2:27). It is also the instrument of correction: “He that spareth his rod hateth his son: but he that loveth him chasteneth him betimes” (Pro 13:24). Micah prays for its pastoral use: “Feed thy people with thy rod, the flock of thine heritage” (Mic 7:14). And a rod in a shepherd's hand became the instrument of a nation's deliverance: “What is that in thine hand? And he said, A rod” (Exo 4:2).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines rod as a shoot or long twig, an instrument of punishment or correction, and, in Scripture, power, authority, and support; and staff as a stick carried in the hand for support, and figuratively, that which props or upholds.
webster_full: ROD, n. The shoot or long twig of any woody plant; a branch, or the shoot of a shrub.
2. An instrument of punishment or correction; discipline; as, to be under the rod.
3. Support; staff.
4. In Scripture, a scepter; hence, power, authority; also, tribe, race.
STAFF, n. A stick carried in the hand for support or defense.
2. A prop; a support; that which props or upholds. Bread is proverbially called the staff of life.
scriptures: Psa 23:4
Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil: for thou art with me; thy rod and thy staff they comfort me.
Rev 2:27
And he shall rule them with a rod of iron; as the vessels of a potter shall they be broken to shivers: even as I received of my Father.
He that spareth his rod hateth his son: but he that loveth him chasteneth him betimes.
Mic 7:14
Feed thy people with thy rod, the flock of thine heritage, which dwell solitarily in the wood, in the midst of Carmel: let them feed in Bashan and Gilead, as in the days of old.
Exo 4:2
And the LORD said unto him, What is that in thine hand? And he said, A rod.
corruption_summary: The rod is read as a threat against the sheep, and in the psalm it is listed among the reasons they are not afraid.
corruption_paragraphs: Psalm 23:4 is precise about the effect of these two objects and it is the opposite of what a modern reader expects: thy rod and thy staff they comfort me. The rod is a club, and in a shepherd's hand it is carried against wolves and thieves rather than swung at the flock. The staff is a crook, used to lift a lamb out of a crevice and to steer an animal drifting toward a drop. Both are instruments of care in the hands of someone competent, and the sheep is comforted by the sight of them because it knows what they are for.

That said, Scripture does not sentimentalise the rod, and Proverbs uses it of correction without apology: he that spareth his rod hateth his son. The logic there is worth stating carefully, because it is a claim about love rather than about severity — the sparing is the hatred, since a child left uncorrected is being abandoned to himself. Hebrews 12 makes the same argument about God's dealings with believers and reaches the conclusion that chastening proves sonship. Nowhere does either passage license anger, and Ephesians 6:4 forbids provoking children to wrath in the same breath as it commands nurture.

Exodus 4:2 puts the whole figure in one question. God asks Moses what is in his hand, and the answer is a rod — an ordinary shepherd's stick, forty years old, the tool of a failed man's obscurity. It becomes the rod that turns a river to blood and divides a sea, and it is still called the rod of God. The pattern is worth noticing by anyone who thinks his equipment is too plain: what was in his hand was what was used.
roots_summary: Hebrew shebet (H7626), rod, sceptre, tribe; mishenet (H4938), staff, support; matteh (H4294), rod, staff, tribe; Greek rhabdos (G4464), a rod, staff, sceptre.
roots_lines: Hebrew shebet (H7626) — rod, club, sceptre, and also tribe; Psalm 23:4, Genesis 49:10, Proverbs 13:24, Micah 7:14.
Hebrew mishenet (H4938) — a staff to lean on; Psalm 23:4, Exodus 21:19, Zechariah 8:4.
Greek rhabdos (G4464) — rod, staff, sceptre; Revelation 2:27, 12:5, 19:15, Hebrews 1:8, 1 Corinthians 4:21.
usage: “Thy rod and thy staff they comfort me” — comfort, from a club and a crook.
“He that spareth his rod hateth his son” — the sparing is the hatred.
“What is that in thine hand?” — and it was an old shepherd's stick.

pos: n. phrase (the whole company of believers, made kings and priests to God, having direct access through Christ)
etymology: Greek basileion hierateuma — a kingly priesthood. Peter lifts the phrase out of Exodus 19:6, where it was said of Israel at Sinai, and applies it to scattered Gentile Christians in Asia Minor.
biblical_def: The royal priesthood is the whole church. Peter states it: “ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people; that ye should shew forth the praises of him who hath called you out of darkness into his marvellous light” (1Pe 2:9). Its function is sacrificial: believers are “an holy priesthood, to offer up spiritual sacrifices, acceptable to God by Jesus Christ” (1Pe 2:5). Its charter is Sinai: “ye shall be unto me a kingdom of priests, and an holy nation” (Exo 19:6). Its purchase is named: He “hath made us kings and priests unto God and his Father” (Rev 1:6). And its privilege is access: “having therefore, brethren, boldness to enter into the holiest by the blood of Jesus… let us draw near” (Heb 10:19–22).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines priesthood as the office or character of a priest; and priest as a person set apart or consecrated to the ministry of the gospel; a man who officiates in sacred offices.
webster_full: PRIESTHOOD, n. The office or character of a priest.
2. The order of men set apart for sacred offices; the order composed of priests.
PRIEST, n. A man who officiates in sacred offices; among Christians, a person consecrated to the ministry of the gospel.
ROYAL, a. Kingly; pertaining to a king; regal; becoming a king; magnificent.
scriptures: But ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people; that ye should shew forth the praises of him who hath called you out of darkness into his marvellous light:
Ye also, as lively stones, are built up a spiritual house, an holy priesthood, to offer up spiritual sacrifices, acceptable to God by Jesus Christ.
Exo 19:6
And ye shall be unto me a kingdom of priests, and an holy nation. These are the words which thou shalt speak unto the children of Israel.
Rev 1:6
And hath made us kings and priests unto God and his Father; to him be glory and dominion for ever and ever. Amen.
Having therefore, brethren, boldness to enter into the holiest by the blood of Jesus,
corruption_summary: The doctrine is used to abolish the ministry, and Peter wrote it to a church that had elders and told them to feed the flock three chapters later.
corruption_paragraphs: The Reformation recovered this doctrine against a system in which a caste stood between God and the people, and its force is exactly what Hebrews 10:19 says: boldness to enter into the holiest. That sentence was unthinkable under the old covenant, where one man entered one room one day a year with blood, and the veil was the point. It was torn from the top down. Every believer now has what only the high priest had, and no human intermediary can improve on the access or is needed to obtain it.

What the doctrine does not do is abolish office, and the same epistle proves it. Peter calls the whole church a royal priesthood in chapter two and in chapter five addresses the elders which are among you, telling them to feed the flock of God and to oversee it. Ephesians 4 says Christ gave pastors and teachers. A universal priesthood and an ordained ministry sit together in the New Testament without strain, because they answer different questions: who may approach God, and who is charged with teaching and governing the congregation.

The neglected half of the doctrine is the duty rather than the privilege. A priest offers, and 1 Peter 2:5 says the sacrifices are spiritual — which the rest of the New Testament itemises: the presenting of one's body a living sacrifice, the sacrifice of praise, the doing good and communicating with which God is well pleased, the offering up of prayer. Most Christians who cherish this doctrine cherish the access clause. Peter's own emphasis in verse 9 is on the output: that ye should shew forth the praises of him who hath called you.
roots_summary: Greek hierateuma (G2406), a priesthood; basileios (G934), royal; parresia (G3954), boldness of access; Hebrew mamleketh kohanim (H4467), a kingdom of priests.
roots_lines: Greek hierateuma (G2406) — priesthood; 1 Peter 2:5, 2:9 — both occurrences, of the whole church.
Greek parresia (G3954) — boldness, freedom of speech and access; Hebrews 10:19, 4:16, Ephesians 3:12, 1 John 4:17.
Hebrew mamleketh kohanim (H4467, H3548) — a kingdom of priests; Exodus 19:6.
usage: “Ye are… a royal priesthood” — written to scattered laymen.
“Boldness to enter into the holiest” — a sentence impossible before the veil tore.
“That ye should shew forth the praises” — the output clause.

pos: n. phrase (the ceasing appointed at creation, commanded at Sinai, fulfilled in Christ, and remaining for the people of God)
etymology: Hebrew shabbath, from shabath, to cease — not primarily to be refreshed but simply to stop. Hebrews coins a Greek word for it, sabbatismos, a sabbath-keeping, used once in the New Testament.
biblical_def: The sabbath rest begins at creation: “And on the seventh day God ended his work which he had made; and he rested on the seventh day from all his work which he had made” (Gen 2:2). It is commanded at Sinai on that ground: “Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy… for in six days the LORD made heaven and earth… and rested the seventh day” (Exo 20:8–11). Its purpose is stated by the Lord: “The sabbath was made for man, and not man for the sabbath” (Mar 2:27). Its substance is Christ: the ordinances “are a shadow of things to come; but the body is of Christ” (Col 2:17). And a rest remains: “There remaineth therefore a rest to the people of God” (Heb 4:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines sabbath as the day which God appointed to be observed by the Jews as a day of rest from all secular labor, and to be kept holy and consecrated to his service; and notes it is also called the Lord's day, observed by Christians on the first day of the week.
webster_full: SABBATH, n. The day which God appointed to be observed by the Jews as a day of rest from all secular labor or employments, and to be kept holy and consecrated to his service and worship.
This day is called the sabbath, or day of rest; and the seventh day of the week was thus consecrated.
2. The day observed by christians as holy time, is the first day of the week, in commemoration of our Savior's resurrection; and hence called the Lord's day.
3. Intermission of pain, effort, sorrow, or the like; as, a sabbath of the mind.
scriptures: Gen 2:2
And on the seventh day God ended his work which he had made; and he rested on the seventh day from all his work which he had made.
Exo 20:8
Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy.
Mar 2:27
And he said unto them, The sabbath was made for man, and not man for the sabbath:
Col 2:17
Which are a shadow of things to come; but the body is of Christ.
Heb 4:9
There remaineth therefore a rest to the people of God.
corruption_summary: The day is defended and the rest is never taken, or the rest is claimed and the day is despised; and the Lord's quarrel was with people who kept it scrupulously.
corruption_paragraphs: Mark 2:27 was spoken in a dispute about disciples pulling ears of corn on the sabbath, and it reverses the whole rabbinic frame: the sabbath was made for man, not man for the sabbath. It is a gift before it is an obligation, given to a people who had just come out of a country where slaves worked without a day off — and Deuteronomy makes that the reason: remember that thou wast a servant in the land of Egypt. Every sabbath argument that ends with people more burdened than they began has lost the verse.

The Reformed have divided on the day and this dictionary states its position plainly: the fourth commandment is moral and abiding, its substance is a day in seven consecrated to God, and its Christian observance is the first day, in commemoration of the resurrection — which is Webster's own account and the confessional one. What must not follow is the elaboration Christ opposed. The Pharisees had built a fence of rules around the day until healing a withered hand inside it became a crime, and He answered them by healing the hand.

Hebrews 4:9 keeps the doctrine from terminating on a calendar. There remaineth a rest to the people of God, and the word is sabbatismos, a sabbath-keeping still ahead. The weekly day is a rehearsal of something not yet possessed, which is why it is kept with rest and worship rather than with mere abstention; and it is also why Colossians 2:17 can call the ordinances a shadow and say the body is of Christ without abolishing the observance. A shadow proves a solid object. The Christian keeps the day looking backward at a finished work and forward at a rest that has not begun.
roots_summary: Hebrew shabath (H7673), to cease, rest; shabbath (H7676), sabbath; Greek sabbatismos (G4520), a sabbath-keeping; skia (G4639), a shadow.
roots_lines: Hebrew shabath (H7673) — to cease, desist; Genesis 2:2–3, Exodus 31:17, Joshua 5:12.
Greek sabbatismos (G4520) — a sabbath rest, a keeping of sabbath; Hebrews 4:9 only.
Greek skia…soma (G4639, G4983) — shadow…body; Colossians 2:17, Hebrews 8:5, 10:1.
usage: “The sabbath was made for man” — a gift before an obligation.
“A shadow of things to come; but the body is of Christ” — and a shadow proves a solid.
“There remaineth therefore a rest” — still ahead.

pos: n. phrase (a holy convocation; the gathering of God's people called together for worship)
etymology: Hebrew miqra qodesh, a holy calling-together — from qara, to call. The assembly is defined by the summons rather than by the attendance: it is holy because God called it.
biblical_def: A sacred assembly is a gathering God calls. The feasts are defined by it: “These are the feasts of the LORD, even holy convocations, which ye shall proclaim in their seasons” (Lev 23:4). In crisis a special one is summoned, and nobody is exempted: “blow the trumpet in Zion, sanctify a fast, call a solemn assembly: Gather the people, sanctify the congregation, assemble the elders, gather the children, and those that suck the breasts” (Joe 2:15–16). The church is commanded not to abandon it: “Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is; but exhorting one another” (Heb 10:25). The pilgrim's gladness is at the summons itself: “I was glad when they said unto me, Let us go into the house of the LORD” (Psa 122:1). And the first church “continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers” (Act 2:42).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines convocation as the act of calling or assembling by summons, and an assembly; and notes the Jewish holy convocation, a solemn assembly on the sabbath and other festivals.
webster_full: CONVOCATION, n. The act of calling or assembling by summons.
2. An assembly.
In the first day there shall be a holy convocation. Ex. 12.
ASSEMBLY, n. A company or collection of individuals, in the same place; usually for the same purpose.
2. A congregation or religious society convened.
scriptures: Lev 23:4
These are the feasts of the LORD, even holy convocations, which ye shall proclaim in their seasons.
Joe 2:15
Blow the trumpet in Zion, sanctify a fast, call a solemn assembly:
Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is; but exhorting one another: and so much the more, as ye see the day approaching.
A Song of degrees of David. I was glad when they said unto me, Let us go into the house of the LORD.
Act 2:42
And they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers.
corruption_summary: Attendance is treated as a preference, and Scripture treats the assembly as a summons with a purpose stated in the same sentence.
corruption_paragraphs: Hebrews 10:25 is quoted constantly and usually stops one clause short. Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is; but exhorting one another: and so much the more, as ye see the day approaching. The command is not merely to be present but to do something while present, and the something is horizontal — exhorting one another. The two verses before it name the reason: to provoke unto love and to good works, which is a thing one Christian does to another and cannot be done at a distance.

Joel 2:16 shows how seriously a solemn assembly was taken by listing who had to come, and the list is deliberately exhausting: the people, the congregation, the elders, the children, and those that suck the breasts. The bridegroom is called out of his chamber and the bride out of her closet, which in that culture meant interrupting a wedding. No category of person is too young, too senior or too newly married to be excused. A congregation that quietly organises itself so that whole categories are absent from its gatherings has drifted from what the word means.

Psalm 122:1 supplies the disposition and it is worth noticing what David is glad about. Not the sermon, not the music, not the company — he is glad when they said unto me, at the summons itself, before anything has happened. That is the mark of a heart in tune with the assembly, and it is also the honest measure of one that is not. The remedy is not more discipline about attendance but the thing Acts 2:42 describes: a gathering worth continuing stedfastly in, built of doctrine, fellowship, bread and prayer.
roots_summary: Hebrew miqra qodesh (H4744, H6944), a holy convocation; atsarah (H6116), a solemn assembly; qahal (H6951), congregation; Greek episunagoge (G1997), an assembling together.
roots_lines: Hebrew miqra qodesh (H4744) — holy convocation; Leviticus 23:2–37, Exodus 12:16, Numbers 28:18.
Hebrew atsarah (H6116) — solemn assembly; Joel 1:14, 2:15, Leviticus 23:36, 2 Kings 10:20.
Greek episunagoge (G1997) — a gathering together; Hebrews 10:25, 2 Thessalonians 2:1.
usage: “But exhorting one another” — the clause usually left off.
“Gather the children, and those that suck the breasts” — nobody excused.
“I was glad when they said unto me” — glad at the summons.

pos: n. phrase (the book sealed with seven seals in Revelation 5, which none but the Lamb was found worthy to open)
etymology: A Roman will or deed was sealed by witnesses and could be opened only by one with legal standing — the heir. That is the legal picture behind the scene: the question is not who is strong enough to break the seals but who has the right.
biblical_def: The sealed scroll appears in the throne room: “And I saw in the right hand of him that sat on the throne a book written within and on the backside, sealed with seven seals” (Rev 5:1). A search is proclaimed and fails: “Who is worthy to open the book, and to loose the seals thereof? And no man in heaven, nor in earth, neither under the earth, was able… And I wept much” (Rev 5:2–4). One is found: “the Lion of the tribe of Juda, the Root of David, hath prevailed to open the book” (Rev 5:5). The ground of His worthiness is named: “Thou art worthy to take the book, and to open the seals thereof: for thou wast slain, and hast redeemed us to God by thy blood” (Rev 5:9). Daniel's book was sealed till the end (Dan 12:4); John's is not: “Seal not the sayings of the prophecy of this book: for the time is at hand” (Rev 22:10).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines seal as a piece of metal or other hard substance used to make an impression, and, figuratively, that which confirms, ratifies or makes stable; assurance; and to seal as to fasten with a seal, to keep secret, to confirm.
webster_full: SEAL, n. A piece of metal or other hard substance, usually round or oval, on which is engraved some image or device, and used to make an impression on wax.
2. That which confirms, ratifies or makes stable; assurance.
3. Any act of confirmation.
SEAL, v.t. To fasten with a seal; to attach together with a wafer or with wax.
2. To set or affix a seal as a mark of authenticity.
3. To confine; to shut up; to keep close.
4. To keep secret.
scriptures: Rev 5:1
And I saw in the right hand of him that sat on the throne a book written within and on the backside, sealed with seven seals.
Rev 5:4
And I wept much, because no man was found worthy to open and to read the book, neither to look thereon.
Rev 5:5
And one of the elders saith unto me, Weep not: behold, the Lion of the tribe of Juda, the Root of David, hath prevailed to open the book, and to loose the seven seals thereof.
Rev 5:9

And they sung a new song, saying, Thou art worthy to take the book, and to open the seals thereof: for thou wast slain, and hast redeemed us to God by thy blood out of every kindred, and tongue, and people, and nation;
And he saith unto me, Seal not the sayings of the prophecy of this book: for the time is at hand.
corruption_summary: The scene is mined for a timetable, and its own drama is a question about worthiness answered by a slain Lamb.
corruption_paragraphs: Revelation 5 is the hinge of the book and it is built as a courtroom scene, not a puzzle. A sealed document lies in the right hand of God; a strong angel proclaims a search through the whole created order — heaven, earth, under the earth — and nobody is found. John's reaction is the detail readers hurry past: and I wept much, because no man was found worthy. An apostle weeping in heaven. Whatever the scroll contains, its remaining shut is a catastrophe, because it means history has no one qualified to carry it forward.

The answer arrives as a contradiction and the contradiction is the doctrine. The elder announces a Lion; John turns and sees a Lamb as it had been slain. The Lion has prevailed — and the way He prevailed is that He was killed. Every theology of power in Scripture converges here: the right to govern history is held by the One who was executed by it, and verse 9 states the qualification without ambiguity, for thou wast slain, and hast redeemed us to God by thy blood. The worthiness is not merely His divine nature; it is His purchase.

The contrast with Daniel is deliberate and closes the canon neatly. Daniel is told to shut up the words and seal the book even to the time of the end; John is told, seal not the sayings of the prophecy of this book: for the time is at hand. What was closed is now open, because the One who could open it has come. That is the answer to every attempt to treat Revelation as a cipher for the initiated: the book announces itself as an unveiling — the word is apokalupsis in its first verse — and pronounces a blessing on the man who merely reads it aloud.
roots_summary: Greek biblion (G975), a book, scroll; sphragis (G4973), a seal; axios (G514), worthy; nikao (G3528), to prevail, overcome.
roots_lines: Greek sphragis (G4973) — a seal; Revelation 5:1–9, 6:1–12, 2 Timothy 2:19, Romans 4:11.
Greek axios (G514) — worthy; Revelation 5:2, 5:4, 5:9, 5:12, 4:11.
Greek enikesen (G3528) — hath prevailed, overcome; Revelation 5:5, 3:21, 17:14.
usage: “And I wept much” — an apostle, in heaven.
“For thou wast slain” — the stated ground of the worthiness.
“Seal not the sayings… for the time is at hand” — against Daniel's instruction.

pos: n. phrase (the lake of fire; the final and irreversible separation from God following the last judgment)
etymology: The phrase is peculiar to Revelation, where it occurs four times, and it presupposes a first death — the body's — which is not final. What the New Testament calls the second death is the one the Lord told men to fear.
biblical_def: The second death is named and defined in one verse: “And death and hell were cast into the lake of fire. This is the second death” (Rev 20:14). Its population is listed: “the fearful, and unbelieving, and the abominable… shall have their part in the lake which burneth with fire and brimstone: which is the second death” (Rev 21:8). Believers are exempt twice over: “He that overcometh shall not be hurt of the second death” (Rev 2:11); and of those in the first resurrection, “on such the second death hath no power” (Rev 20:6). The Lord fixes the proportion between the two deaths: “fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul: but rather fear him which is able to destroy both soul and body in hell” (Mat 10:28).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines the second death as the everlasting separation of the wicked from the presence and favor of God; and death, in a theological sense, as perpetual separation from God, and eternal torments.
webster_full: DEATH, n. That state of a being, animal or vegetable, in which there is a total and permanent cessation of all the vital functions.
2. In theology, perpetual separation from God, and eternal torments; called the second death.
3. Separation or alienation of the soul from God; a being under the dominion of sin, and destitute of grace or divine life; called spiritual death.
The wages of sin is death. Rom. 6.
scriptures: And death and hell were cast into the lake of fire. This is the second death.
Rev 21:8

But the fearful, and unbelieving, and the abominable, and murderers, and whoremongers, and sorcerers, and idolaters, and all liars, shall have their part in the lake which burneth with fire and brimstone: which is the second death.
Rev 2:11
He that hath an ear, let him hear what the Spirit saith unto the churches; He that overcometh shall not be hurt of the second death.
Rev 20:6
Blessed and holy is he that hath part in the first resurrection: on such the second death hath no power, but they shall be priests of God and of Christ, and shall reign with him a thousand years.
And fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul: but rather fear him which is able to destroy both soul and body in hell.
corruption_summary: The doctrine is either softened out of existence or handled with a relish, and Scripture states it soberly and offers an escape in the same book.
corruption_paragraphs: Matthew 10:28 is the Lord's own calibration and it is addressed to disciples being sent into danger. Fear not them which kill the body — that is the first death, and He tells them not to be afraid of it — but rather fear him which is able to destroy both soul and body in hell. The verse relativises martyrdom and absolutises the second death in one sentence. Whatever a Christian believes about the details, he cannot hold the doctrine lightly and still be reading the same Teacher who said this, and it is worth noticing that He said it as an encouragement.

The two errors are equal and opposite. One dissolves the doctrine, generally out of a real and creditable horror at the thought — and ends by making the cross unintelligible, since it is hard to say what Christ was rescuing anyone from. The other handles it with evident satisfaction, which is a far uglier fault, and one that Ezekiel forecloses: As I live, saith the Lord GOD, I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked. A man who can speak of the second death without any tremor has not understood it, whichever direction his error runs.

Revelation 21:8 rewards close reading for who heads the list. Not the murderers or the sorcerers first — the fearful, and unbelieving. The cowardly. In a book written to churches under Roman pressure, the sin named first among the lost is the failure of nerve that denies Christ to stay safe, which is the same sin Revelation 2:11 promises the overcomer will escape. And the immediately preceding verse is the offer: I will give unto him that is athirst of the fountain of the water of life freely. The chapter puts the invitation next to the warning, and so should anyone teaching it.
roots_summary: Greek ho thanatos ho deuteros (G2288), the second death; limne tou puros (G3041), the lake of fire; apollumi (G622), to destroy; nikao (G3528), to overcome.
roots_lines: Greek ho deuteros thanatos (G1208, G2288) — the second death; Revelation 2:11, 20:6, 20:14, 21:8 — all four occurrences.
Greek limne tou puros (G3041) — the lake of fire; Revelation 19:20, 20:10, 20:14–15, 21:8.
Greek apolesai (G622) — to destroy; Matthew 10:28, James 4:12.
usage: “This is the second death” — defined in one clause.
“The fearful, and unbelieving” — heading the list, in a persecuted church's book.
“On such the second death hath no power” — no power, not merely no sentence.

pos: n. phrase (the covering protection of God, figured as shade in a hot country and as the shadow of a bird's wings)
etymology: Hebrew tsel, a shadow — and in the climate the psalms come from, shade is not gloom but survival. The associated figure is kanaph, a wing: the shadow is cast by something spread over the one sheltering.
biblical_def: The shadow of the Almighty is God's covering: “He that dwelleth in the secret place of the most High shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty” (Psa 91:1). The figure is usually a wing: “Keep me as the apple of the eye, hide me under the shadow of thy wings” (Psa 17:8); “therefore the children of men put their trust under the shadow of thy wings” (Psa 36:7); “Because thou hast been my help, therefore in the shadow of thy wings will I rejoice” (Psa 63:7). And Isaiah gives the plainest reason a shadow matters: God has been “a strength to the poor, a strength to the needy in his distress, a refuge from the storm, a shadow from the heat” (Isa 25:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines shadow as shade within defined limits, and, figuratively, protection; shelter; favor; and notes the Scriptural use, to be under the shadow of the Almighty.
webster_full: SHADOW, n. Shade within defined limits; obscurity or deprivation of light, apparent on a plane and representing the form of the body which intercepts the rays of light.
2. Darkness; shade; obscurity.
3. Shelter made by any thing that intercepts the light, heat or influence of the air.
4. Obscure place; secluded retreat.
5. Protection; shelter; favor. Hide me under the shadow of thy wings. Ps. 17.
scriptures: Psa 91:1
He that dwelleth in the secret place of the most High shall abide under the shadow of the Almighty.
Psa 17:8
Keep me as the apple of the eye, hide me under the shadow of thy wings,
Psa 36:7
How excellent is thy lovingkindness, O God! therefore the children of men put their trust under the shadow of thy wings.
Psa 63:7
Because thou hast been my help, therefore in the shadow of thy wings will I rejoice.
Isa 25:4

For thou hast been a strength to the poor, a strength to the needy in his distress, a refuge from the storm, a shadow from the heat, when the blast of the terrible ones is as a storm against the wall.
corruption_summary: Psalm 91 is read as a guarantee against harm, and it was quoted to Christ by the devil for exactly that purpose.
corruption_paragraphs: Psalm 91 is the one psalm Scripture records Satan quoting, and he quotes it accurately: he shall give his angels charge over thee, to keep thee in all thy ways. The misuse is not in the words but in the application — an invitation to jump off a pinnacle and require God to catch him. The Lord's answer is not a denial of the psalm but another verse: thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God. A promise of protection is not a licence to manufacture the danger, and any reading of Psalm 91 that produces recklessness has been used the way the tempter used it.

The psalm also has to be read alongside the rest of the canon, where the men who trusted God most were sawn asunder, stoned, and slain with the sword — and Hebrews 11 lists them among the commended. Whatever Psalm 91 promises, it does not promise exemption from suffering to everyone in every case, or the martyrs were outside the covenant. What it promises is a shelter that holds through the thing rather than around it, which is the same distinction Psalm 23 makes by walking through the valley rather than around it.

The strength of the figure is in the physics. A shadow requires a body between you and the source of the heat, close enough and large enough to cover you, and it moves when that body moves — which is why the psalm's first line is about dwelling and abiding rather than visiting. Isaiah 25:4 names what the shade is for: a refuge from the storm, a shadow from the heat, when the blast of the terrible ones is as a storm against the wall. It is protection in the middle of weather, not the absence of weather.
roots_summary: Hebrew tsel (H6738), shadow, shade; kanaph (H3671), wing, edge; Shaddai (H7706), the Almighty; sether (H5643), a secret place, covering.
roots_lines: Hebrew tsel Shaddai (H6738, H7706) — the shadow of the Almighty; Psalm 91:1.
Hebrew tsel kenapheka (H3671) — the shadow of thy wings; Psalm 17:8, 36:7, 57:1, 63:7.
Hebrew sether (H5643) — secret place, covering; Psalm 91:1, 27:5, 32:7, 119:114.
usage: “Shall abide under the shadow” — abide, which is why the first clause is dwelleth.
“Hide me under the shadow of thy wings” — something spread over.
“A refuge from the storm, a shadow from the heat” — in the weather, not out of it.

pos: n. phrase (Psalm 23; the best-known passage in the Old Testament, written by a shepherd about a Shepherd)
etymology: The title is not in the text; it was given by readers. The psalm's own opening word in Hebrew is YHWH ro'i — the LORD is my shepherd — and the metaphor was a royal one throughout the ancient near east, which is part of its force from a king's pen.
biblical_def: The Shepherd Psalm opens with a claim and a consequence: “The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want” (Psa 23:1). Its centre is the valley: “Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil: for thou art with me; thy rod and thy staff they comfort me” (Psa 23:4). Christ takes the title and adds what no shepherd of Israel had done: “I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep” (John 10:11). Ezekiel had promised God would do the work Himself: “Behold, I, even I, will both search my sheep, and seek them out” (Eze 34:11). And Peter names the last appearing: “when the chief Shepherd shall appear, ye shall receive a crown of glory that fadeth not away” (1Pe 5:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines shepherd as a man employed in tending, feeding and guarding sheep in the field; and, in a spiritual sense, a minister of the gospel, or, of Christ, the great Shepherd and Bishop of souls.
webster_full: SHEPHERD, n. A man employed in tending, feeding and guarding sheep in the field.
2. A swain; a rural lover.
3. The pastor of a church; one who exercises the pastoral office.
The Lord is my shepherd; I shall not want. Ps. 23.
PASTOR, n. A shepherd; one that has the care of flocks and herds.
2. A minister of the gospel who has the charge of a church and congregation.
scriptures: Psa 23:1
A Psalm of David. The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want.
Psa 23:4
Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil: for thou art with me; thy rod and thy staff they comfort me.
John 10:11
I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep.
For thus saith the Lord GOD; Behold, I, even I, will both search my sheep, and seek them out.
And when the chief Shepherd shall appear, ye shall receive a crown of glory that fadeth not away.
corruption_summary: The psalm is heard as a pastoral idyll, and it contains a valley, an enemy and a table set in front of them.
corruption_paragraphs: The psalm is read at funerals so often that its edges have worn off, and the edges are what make it worth reading. There is a valley of the shadow of death and the sheep goes through it — not around, and the shepherd's answer to it is not a diversion but a presence: for thou art with me. There is a table prepared in the presence of mine enemies, who are still present at the meal. And the implements that comfort are a club and a crook, which are carried because something out there requires them.

The claim in the first verse is also stronger than it sounds in English. I shall not want is not a promise of prosperity; it is a statement about a shepherd's competence, and the following verses itemise the provision — green pastures, still waters, a restored soul, right paths — each of which a sheep is incapable of finding for itself. That is the point of the metaphor and it is not flattering. Isaiah's summary of the human condition uses the same animal: all we like sheep have gone astray, we have turned every one to his own way.

David wrote it as a shepherd and as a king, and the second is what makes John 10 land. In the ancient near east shepherd was a royal title, and Ezekiel 34 is a furious oracle against the shepherds of Israel who fed themselves and not the flock, ending with God's promise to come and do it Himself. Then a Galilean says, I am the good shepherd, and adds the one thing no king had ever included in the job description: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep.
roots_summary: Hebrew ro'eh (H7462), a shepherd, one who feeds; tsalmaveth (H6757), the shadow of death; Greek poimen (G4166), shepherd; archipoimen (G750), chief Shepherd.
roots_lines: Hebrew ro'eh (H7462) — shepherd, to feed, tend; Psalm 23:1, Ezekiel 34:2–23, Isaiah 40:11.
Hebrew tsalmaveth (H6757) — deep shadow, shadow of death; Psalm 23:4, Job 3:5, 10:21, Isaiah 9:2.
Greek archipoimen (G750) — chief Shepherd; 1 Peter 5:4 only.
usage: “Though I walk through the valley” — through, and not around.
“In the presence of mine enemies” — still present, at the table.
“The good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep” — not in any king's job description.
related: Valley of the Shadow of Death

pos: n. (the ram's-horn trumpet of Israel, sounded to assemble, to alarm, to enthrone, and to announce the day of the LORD)
etymology: Hebrew shophar, a ram's horn, distinguished in the Law from the chatsotserah, the beaten silver trumpet. The horn is the older and rougher instrument, and it is the one that sounds at Sinai and at Jericho.
biblical_def: The trumpet summons. Two silver trumpets are made “for the calling of the assembly, and for the journeying of the camps” (Num 10:2). The horn opens the year of release: “then shalt thou cause the trumpet of the jubile to sound… and ye shall hallow the fiftieth year, and proclaim liberty throughout all the land” (Lev 25:9–10). It brings down a city: “when the people heard the sound of the trumpet, and the people shouted with a great shout, that the wall fell down flat” (Jos 6:20). And it sounds at the end: “the Lord himself shall descend from heaven with a shout, with the voice of the archangel, and with the trump of God” (1Th 4:16); “at the last trump: for the trumpet shall sound, and the dead shall be raised incorruptible” (1Co 15:52).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines trumpet as a wind instrument of music, used chiefly in war and military exercises, and notes its Scriptural use to assemble the congregation, to sound an alarm, and to proclaim the jubilee.
webster_full: TRUMPET, n. A wind instrument of music, used chiefly in war and military exercises, as in war and in assembling the people.
The trumpet was used among the Israelites to assemble the people, to sound an alarm, to proclaim the jubilee, and in religious festivals.
2. In military affairs, a trumpeter.
3. One who praises or propagates praise, or is the instrument of propagating it.
scriptures: Num 10:2
Make thee two trumpets of silver; of a whole piece shalt thou make them: that thou mayest use them for the calling of the assembly, and for the journeying of the camps.
Lev 25:9
Then shalt thou cause the trumpet of the jubile to sound on the tenth day of the seventh month, in the day of atonement shall ye make the trumpet sound throughout all your land.
Jos 6:20

So the people shouted when the priests blew with the trumpets: and it came to pass, when the people heard the sound of the trumpet, and the people shouted with a great shout, that the wall fell down flat, so that the people went up into the city, every man straight before him, and they took the city.
For the Lord himself shall descend from heaven with a shout, with the voice of the archangel, and with the trump of God: and the dead in Christ shall rise first:
In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trump: for the trumpet shall sound, and the dead shall be raised incorruptible, and we shall be changed.
corruption_summary: The trumpet is treated as ceremony, and every use Scripture records is a signal that required somebody to move.
corruption_paragraphs: Numbers 10 is the passage that governs the rest, and it establishes that a trumpet is a language. One trumpet gathered the princes; two gathered the whole assembly; a different blast — an alarm — struck the camps and set them journeying. Paul reaches for exactly this when arguing about intelligible speech in the church: if the trumpet give an uncertain sound, who shall prepare himself to the battle? The instrument's whole value is that a listener knows what is being asked of him, which makes it a good figure for preaching and a poor one for atmosphere.

The jubilee blast is the most remarkable of them. On the day of atonement of the fiftieth year the horn sounded and the economy reset: debts released, slaves freed, land returned to the family that had lost it. Liberty was proclaimed throughout all the land unto all the inhabitants thereof — the sentence on the Liberty Bell — and it began with a sound rather than a negotiation. It is difficult to read Leviticus 25 without noticing how little of it Israel ever kept, and how exactly it describes what the gospel claims to have done.

Jericho is the case that resists every attempt at a natural explanation, and the text is unembarrassed: they marched, the priests blew, the people shouted, and the wall fell down flat. Hebrews 11 lists it among the works of faith. What the narrative is careful to include is the six days of walking in silence beforehand, which must have looked ridiculous to everyone on the wall. Most obedience of this kind looks that way until the seventh day.
roots_summary: Hebrew shophar (H7782), a ram's-horn trumpet; chatsotserah (H2689), a silver trumpet; teruah (H8643), a shout, alarm blast; Greek salpigx (G4536), a trumpet.
roots_lines: Hebrew shophar (H7782) — ram's horn; Leviticus 25:9, Joshua 6:4–20, Exodus 19:16, Psalm 47:5.
Hebrew chatsotserah (H2689) — silver trumpet; Numbers 10:2–10, 2 Chronicles 5:12.
Greek salpigx (G4536) — trumpet; 1 Corinthians 15:52, 1 Thessalonians 4:16, Matthew 24:31, Revelation 8:2.
usage: “For the calling of the assembly, and for the journeying” — a language, not a noise.
“Proclaim liberty throughout all the land” — and it began with a sound.
“The trumpet shall sound, and the dead shall be raised”.

pos: n. phrase (the experience of praying and receiving no answer; God's hiddenness as Scripture itself describes it)
etymology: The Bible has no single term for this; it has a vocabulary of complaint — how long, why standest thou afar off, thou hearest not — and it puts that vocabulary in the mouths of its most faithful men, and into the Psalter for congregational use.
biblical_def: The silence of God is a recorded experience of the faithful. David: “O my God, I cry in the daytime, but thou hearest not; and in the night season, and am not silent” (Psa 22:2). Again: “How long wilt thou forget me, O LORD? for ever? how long wilt thou hide thy face from me?” (Psa 13:1). Habakkuk opens his book with it: “O LORD, how long shall I cry, and thou wilt not hear!” (Hab 1:2). Job searches in every direction: “Behold, I go forward, but he is not there; and backward, but I cannot perceive him” (Job 23:8). And Isaiah says it of God without reproach: “Verily thou art a God that hidest thyself, O God of Israel, the Saviour” (Isa 45:15).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines silence as stillness; the state of a person or thing not speaking; and, of God, forbearance of speech; and hiddenness as the state of being concealed.
webster_full: SILENCE, n. In a general sense, stillness, or entire absence of sound or noise.
2. The state of a person or thing not speaking; forbearance of speech in man.
3. Habitual taciturnity; opposed to loquacity.
4. Oblivion; obscurity.
HIDE, v.t. To conceal; to withhold or withdraw from sight.
scriptures: Psa 22:2
O my God, I cry in the daytime, but thou hearest not; and in the night season, and am not silent.
Psa 13:1
To the chief Musician, A Psalm of David. How long wilt thou forget me, O LORD? for ever? how long wilt thou hide thy face from me?
Hab 1:2
O LORD, how long shall I cry, and thou wilt not hear! even cry out unto thee of violence, and thou wilt not save!
Job 23:8
Behold, I go forward, but he is not there; and backward, but I cannot perceive him:
Verily thou art a God that hidest thyself, O God of Israel, the Saviour.
corruption_summary: Silence is treated as evidence of God's absence or of the believer's failure, and Scripture gives it to its best men and puts their complaints in the hymnbook.
corruption_paragraphs: The first thing to say is that the complaint is canonical. Psalm 13 begins with four how longs and Psalm 22 with why hast thou forsaken me, and these were not private notes — they were given to the chief Musician, for public singing. A tradition that has no vocabulary for unanswered prayer has edited its own hymnbook, and it leaves sufferers with the impression that their experience is unusual and disgraceful when it is neither. Roughly a third of the Psalter is lament.

The second thing is what those psalms do with the silence, because they do not stay in it and they do not resolve it cheaply either. Psalm 13 turns at verse 5 — but I have trusted in thy mercy — without anything having changed in the circumstances. Psalm 22 moves from forsakenness to thou hast heard me and ends with the ends of the world remembering and turning to the LORD. Job 23 is the model of honest searching: he cannot find God in any direction, and in the same breath says, but he knoweth the way that I take: when he hath tried me, I shall come forth as gold.

The third thing is the one that finally answers it. Psalm 22:2 is quoted from the cross, and there the silence was real and total and undeserved: My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me? Whatever a believer experiences of God's hiddenness, it is not the abandonment Christ bore, and it is not the same thing because that one was. Hebrews says of Him that in the days of his flesh he offered up prayers and supplications with strong crying and tears, and was heard — and the answer, that time, came after the grave. Isaiah 45:15 is the sober statement of the doctrine and it does not apologise: thou art a God that hidest thyself — and the same clause calls Him the Saviour.
roots_summary: Hebrew ad-anah (H575), how long; sathar (H5641), to hide; azab (H5800), to forsake; Greek egkataleipo (G1459), to abandon.
roots_lines: Hebrew ad-anah (H575) — how long; Psalm 13:1–2, Habakkuk 1:2, Job 18:2, Exodus 16:28.
Hebrew sathar panim (H5641) — to hide the face; Psalm 13:1, 27:9, 88:14, Isaiah 45:15, 54:8.
Greek egkatelipes (G1459) — hast thou forsaken; Matthew 27:46, Mark 15:34, quoting Psalm 22:1.
usage: “I cry in the daytime, but thou hearest not” — given to the chief Musician.
“He knoweth the way that I take” — said by a man who could not find Him.
“Thou art a God that hidest thyself… the Saviour” — both, in one clause.
